source_document.body:
Photo: © Makidotvn
By Charlotte Goldstone
27 November 2026
Air cargo rates continue to face upward pressure as capacity constraints, rather than a surge in peak season demand, increasingly dictate pricing – with freighter capacity into Europe taking a significant hit ahead of Black Friday.
Data published today by aviation consultant Aevean shows freighter capacity from Asia and the Middle East into Europe fell 15% year on year in the two weeks to 24 November, equivalent to some 27,500 tonnes.
“Black Friday… or Red Friday?” asked Maarten Wormer, head of consulting at Aevean, noting that “integrator and general cargo hubs are largely holding up, as ecommerce gateways take the hit”.
Budapest recorded the steepest percentage decline among the eight major gateways tracked, at 36%, followed by Paris CDG, down 27%, and Liège, down 24% – the latter losing some 5,800 tonnes of capacity.
Meanwhile, Frankfurt saw an 11% reduction, while Cologne bucked the trend with a 16% increase. Capacity into Amsterdam remained flat.
The figures come amid a resurgence in global airfreight rates, following a period of easing in the third quarter.
According to Transport Intelligence’s (Ti) latest Air Freight Rate Tracker, global headhaul rates reached $3.92 per kg in early November, up 7.6% on October, 8.7% against the Q3 average, and 45.2% year on year.
Backhaul rates climbed 6.2% month on month, to $3 per kg, up 22.3% year on year.
However, it is the withdrawal of bellyhold capacity during winter passenger schedules, coupled with persistently high fuel costs, rather than exceptional demand growth, that Ti identified as driving the increases.
Westbound transatlantic rates recorded the largest quarterly increase, at 21.7%, largely reflecting seasonal capacity reductions.
But technology shipments continue to underpin demand elsewhere, with South Asia-North America remaining the most expensive tradelane tracked by Ti, at $7.08 per kg, up 70.5% year on year. And the strength of demand for AI infrastructure, servers and semiconductors could see freighters redeployed to the Transpacific, further tightening capacity elsewhere.
Meanwhile, there is little consensus over whether shippers can expect much respite in the new year.
Despite 72% of respondents to Ti’s industry survey anticipating rate increases over the next three months, the consultant expects prices to ease in Q1 27, recalling that rates fell between Q4 and Q1 in each of the past four years.
Some 81% of respondents expected increases on the Asia-US West Coast trade.
While softer e-commerce, consumer, and industrial demand following the peak season should weigh on pricing, sustained technology shipments and limited capacity are expected to cushion any decline.
Ti also suggested shippers should avoid locking-in November rates on 12-month contracts – shorter-term agreements or index-linked pricing potentially offering greater flexibility.
And Transatlantic shippers could benefit from delaying tenders until the return of summer passenger schedules in late March, when the additional bellyhold capacity could bring some relief.
